title: Dēpology Design System
subtitle: Turning mobile commerce friction into reusable navigation, buybox, cart, checkout, and responsive product-page patterns.
problem: Depology, a rapidly growing Korean skincare brand with a strong Instagram presence in the US market, was preparing to launch multiple new products for shadow testing through paid advertising. They needed optimized product landing pages to maximize conversion rates in their ad-to-web customer journey. However, initial analysis revealed critical friction points: heatmap data showed users struggling with the mobile product buybox, while analytics indicated high drop-off rates and shortened session lengths tied to confusing header navigation on mobile devices. These UX issues were directly hindering conversion potential at a crucial growth moment.
solution: A data-driven redesign focused on the two highest-impact friction points: the mobile buybox and header navigation. After conducting thorough analysis of heatmaps, conversion funnels, and session behavior, new designs were proposed and validated through A/B testing. The redesigned mobile buybox streamlined the purchase flow with clearer CTAs and improved information hierarchy, while the simplified header navigation reduced cognitive load and improved discoverability. Following successful test runs and stakeholder presentations that secured buy-in from both product and marketing leadership, the changes were implemented across new product landing pages and ultimately adopted site-wide.
body: Depology was at an inflection point. The Korean skincare brand had built a devoted following on Instagram and was ready to scale through aggressive product launches and paid advertising. But there was a problem: their existing product pages weren't converting at the rates needed to justify increased ad spend. With multiple new products queued for shadow testing—a strategy where products are launched quietly to gauge market response before full rollout—the team needed landing pages that could turn Instagram traffic into customers efficiently.

The first step was diagnosis. Heatmap analysis revealed that mobile users were tapping repeatedly on elements within the product buybox, suggesting confusion about how to add items to cart or select variants. Conversion funnel data confirmed the suspicion: a significant percentage of users were abandoning their sessions at the product page stage. Session length metrics told another story—users who did engage were spending less time on site than expected, often bouncing after encountering the cluttered header navigation. These weren't assumptions; they were patterns backed by behavioral data.

Armed with these insights, the redesign focused on surgical improvements rather than wholesale changes. The mobile buybox was reimagined with a clearer visual hierarchy: variant selectors were made more prominent, the add-to-cart button was enlarged and repositioned for thumb-friendly access, and product information was reorganized to answer questions in the order customers naturally asked them. The header navigation was simplified dramatically, reducing menu options and improving the information architecture to help users find what they needed without overwhelming them. Every decision was testable, measurable, and directly tied to observed user behavior.

The validation process was methodical. Test runs were launched on select product pages, with conversion rates monitored daily. The results were striking: the new designs drove a conversion rate increase that validated every hypothesis. With data in hand, the pitch to product and marketing leadership was straightforward—these changes weren't subjective design preferences, they were proven performance improvements. The stakeholders backed the rollout, and the new UI was implemented first across all new product landing pages, then gradually adopted across the entire site. Depology's mobile experience had transformed from a conversion bottleneck into a growth engine.

title: Explainable Property Search
subtitle: A technical UX case study translating ambiguous renter language into editable intent, ranked recommendations, and inspectable Python + JSON search logic.
problem: Property seekers often describe intent in natural language, but standard filters split that intent across separate controls and leave users unsure whether the system understood their requirements.
solution: A mobile-first NLP search flow that turns renter language into editable chips, runs against a Python-backed ranking layer and structured JSON property data, then explains matches in the interface.

title: Worldschooling
subtitle: A launch-ready education-travel platform that narrowed a large booking vision into programme comparison, eligibility checks, and deposit confidence.
problem: Worldschooling did not just need a nicer website. The real problem was release scope. The team wanted a full education-travel platform with campus pages, subject pages, programme pages, search, blog, booking, and payment, but that level of build would have slowed down the launch at the exact moment the company needed something usable for fundraising, sales conversations, and early customer enquiries. I treated the first release as a decision problem rather than a page-count problem: before a parent pays a deposit, they need to compare programme types, understand whether the trip is suitable, check the level of commitment, and know what information the team needs from them.
solution: I simplified the first-release journey around the decisions that had to happen before commitment: programme discovery, tier comparison, programme detail, eligibility form, and a universal deposit link. This was less automated than a custom booking portal, but it kept the important customer steps visible and removed months of engineering scope. The homepage category selector made mid-tier programmes easier to discover before users were deep in the site, while recommendation cards on entry-level pages made the next tier visible where comparison already made sense.
body: The project started with a scope problem hiding inside a website brief. The planned platform had enough pieces to become a long product build: campus pages, subject pages, programme pages, search, blog, booking portal, and payment. For an early-stage education-travel business, that would have delayed the thing the team needed most: a credible surface that could explain programmes and support conversations with parents, students, and stakeholders.

I looked at the journey from the parent side first. A parent does not start by asking whether the site has a custom booking engine. They ask what the programme is, whether it fits their child, what is included, what the commitment is, and what happens after they submit details. That changed the structure of the first release. The booking portal became less important than comparison, eligibility, and deposit clarity.

The design choice was to replace the first-release booking engine with a simpler path: homepage, programme filtering, detail pages, eligibility form, and a universal deposit payment link. The tradeoff was clear. The flow was less automated for the business, but it made the product launchable and kept the important decision points visible to customers.

I used the homepage to expose programme categories rather than burying the range behind static cards. The selector gave users a way to move between themes and levels, while the detail pages carried the specific confidence cues: what the programme includes, who it is for, and what the next step requires. Recommendation cards on entry-level pages introduced higher-value options where comparison already made sense.

The outcome I would claim is launch readiness, not proven conversion. The new structure gave the team a usable sales and fundraising surface without waiting for a full booking platform. The next thing I would inspect is the live funnel: which programme categories people open, where parents leave the eligibility form, and whether recommendation cards actually lead to deposit clicks or just extra browsing.

title: Worldover.io
subtitle: A compliance command-centre case study turning threshold risk, entity scope, production evidence, alerts, and report blockers into one scannable decision workflow.
problem: Compliance teams need to move between different kinds of thinking: risk triage, production review, alert setup, report readiness, and evidence audit. The earlier dashboard direction made the system feel data-rich, but it blurred those mindspaces and made it harder to see what action would actually clear a threshold breach.
solution: I redesigned the experience around a multi-tab command flow. Each tab preserves a separate mental mode, while the Risk Command tab simplifies the core decision into detect, decide, and assign. The prototype is backed by dummy structured data so entity and chemical changes alter severity, metrics, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and close checks.

content.value: Worldover operates in a high-consequence compliance space where users need confidence before acting. A single annual threshold breach can involve production plans, legal entity scope, registration limits, stale data, plant owners, evidence imports, and report-generation blockers. The product challenge was not simply showing more information. It was helping a user know which kind of work they were doing at any moment.

content.title: Why the live demo looks different from the original delivery
content.value: The embedded Risk Command Centre is a recent April 2026 update of the earlier Worldover delivery. The original work established the compliance dashboard direction and visual system; this newer demo revisits the same product problem with a more operational lens. I kept the domain, compliance logic, and Worldover brand cues, but rebuilt the experience to show how the product could move from monitoring data to resolving threshold risk. That is why the live demo intentionally looks and behaves differently from the older dashboard screens.

content.title: Risk Command Centre
content.description: Change the entity selector to see the backend display conditions switch across the whole interface: case status, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and readiness all update from the dummy data model.

content.kicker: What improved from the old delivery
content.title: Five design upgrades in the April 2026 demo

items.title: From passive dashboard to action command centre
items.value: The older delivery focused on surfacing compliance data. The updated demo turns the same risk context into a guided workflow: detect the signal, decide the mitigation, assign the next owner, and watch readiness change.

items.title: Clearer mindspace separation
items.value: Risk Command, Production, Alerts, Reporting, and Evidence now live in separate tabs. This preserves context for different user tasks instead of mixing tables, charts, rules, and audit records into one overloaded screen.

items.title: Entity-aware data behavior
items.value: The prototype is backed by structured dummy data with entity-specific display conditions. Switching from group view to Germany, France, or UK changes severity, metrics, readiness, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and the resolution drawer.

items.title: Sharper compliance storytelling
items.value: The case now communicates not just what is above threshold, but why it matters, what is blocking closure, who owns the next action, and what evidence is still missing before reporting can proceed.

items.title: More polished production-facing interaction design
items.value: The April 2026 demo applies a tighter Worldover-inspired visual language, better text hierarchy, resolved z-index/layout issues, accessible real threshold labels, and browser-tested responsive behavior.

content.value: The main UX decision was to keep multiple tabs rather than collapse everything into one mega-dashboard. Risk Command is for deciding what to do. Production is for factory contribution and threshold consumption. Alerts are for rules and escalation. Reporting is for blockers and draft gates. Evidence is for imports and audit trail. That separation makes the interface calmer because each tab has one job.

Inside Risk Command, the flow is intentionally narrow: detect the signal, decide the mitigation, then assign the work. This reduces the cognitive load for a compliance operator who may be under deadline pressure. The UI still exposes supporting data, but it does not ask the user to interpret every table before taking the next step.

content.caption: The case study reframes Worldover from a static compliance dashboard into an operational command centre with clearer mode separation.

content.value: To make the prototype realistic, I mapped a dummy backend payload that covers the display states the interface needs: severity classes, readiness rules, chemical records, entity views, production charts, alert rules, reporting sections, evidence records, drawer actions, and empty states. Entity selection is no longer a label-only filter; it changes the full display context.

title: Travel to Qin
subtitle: A trust-building travel site for international visitors who needed itinerary clarity before enquiring about China trips.
problem: Travel to Qin did not simply need a more beautiful travel site. The old Shopify page could take a transaction, but it did not answer the questions a foreign visitor needs answered before trusting a China itinerary: who runs the trip, what the experience actually includes, how support works, why the agency is credible, and what happens after enquiry. The September 2024 visa policy change made the opportunity clearer, but it also raised the standard for trust.
solution: I rebuilt the experience around proof before purchase. The new structure used a video-led opening for immediate context, then moved into destination sections, itinerary details, service explanations, and an enquiry path. The CMS decision mattered because the team needed to update trips, stories, and campaign content without redesigning the site each time. The visual direction used Chinese calligraphy and landscape references, but the goal was not decoration; the brand system had to carry cultural atmosphere and service clarity at the same time.
body: The original site problem was not that it lacked visual polish. It was that the page behaved like a checkout before the visitor had enough reasons to trust the trip. A foreign traveller considering China needs context before commitment: what they will see, who will guide them, how the itinerary is organised, what support exists, and why this agency is credible.

I looked at the site as a trust sequence. The first screen needed to make the destination feel real, but the rest of the page needed to answer practical questions. Beautiful imagery could create interest, but it could not carry the whole job. The content order had to move visitors from inspiration to understanding to enquiry.

The design direction was to put proof before purchase. I used a video-led opening to establish place and scale, then built sections for itinerary structure, destination context, service explanation, and next-step clarity. This gave the visitor a reason to keep reading instead of landing directly on a transaction page with too many unanswered questions.

The brand work followed the same logic. Chinese calligraphy and landscape references gave the identity cultural grounding, while the colour palette, typography, cards, and layout system made the information easier to scan. I wanted the site to feel connected to China without turning into a poster. The brand had to support the service, not sit on top of it.

Moving from Shopify to a CMS was a practical choice, not just a technical upgrade. Travel content changes: itineraries, seasonal campaigns, stories, and destination highlights all need editing. A CMS gave the team a way to keep the site current without rebuilding the page for every campaign.

The outcome I would claim is a stronger trust and sales surface, not automatic conversion uplift. The work gave stakeholders a site that could support social traffic, brochures, and future app surfaces with one visual language. The next thing I would inspect is where visitors pause, which itinerary sections they read, which social channels send qualified enquiries, and what questions still appear before someone contacts the team.

images.caption: The redesign moved the site from transaction-first checkout to a trust-building travel surface with destination context, itinerary detail, and enquiry clarity.
The page structure answers pre-enquiry questions in order: what the trip feels like, what is included, why the agency is credible, and what to do next.
Itinerary content was treated as proof, not decoration. The brochure format helps visitors understand the trip before speaking to the team.
The identity uses Chinese visual references while keeping the system practical enough for service information, campaigns, and future product surfaces.
Destination cards break the travel offer into scannable choices so visitors can compare places before enquiring.
The print system extends the same trust sequence into offline sales material: context first, itinerary proof second, enquiry path last.

title: TUTU FUTURE
subtitle: a strategic rebrand for a Chinese study tour operator expanding beyond hiking trips into academic and cultural programs.
problem: TUTU FUTURE, a study tour operator specializing in short-term European programs for Chinese students, had outgrown its original brand identity. The existing logo and visual system were built around a student hiking theme with green color palette—appropriate for their early adventure-focused tours but increasingly misaligned as they expanded into academic courses, art programs, STEM workshops, and language immersion experiences. The hiking-centric brand failed to communicate the breadth and sophistication of their evolving offerings, limiting their appeal to prospective students seeking diverse educational experiences in Europe.
solution: A comprehensive brand refresh that repositioned TUTU FUTURE from an outdoor adventure operator to a multifaceted educational travel platform. The new visual identity system included a modernized logo that balanced academic credibility with youthful energy, an expanded color palette that could flex across different program types (art, STEM, language, culture), and a complete suite of marketing materials optimized for social media campaigns. A custom mascot design added approachability and personality, while the new tone of voice guidelines ensured consistent communication across all touchpoints. The scalable system empowered the team to create cohesive materials for any program type without redesigning from scratch.
body: TUTU FUTURE's challenge was one of evolution. They had built a loyal following among Chinese students seeking European adventure, but their ambitions had grown beyond hiking trails. As they added academic programs, art workshops, STEM courses, and language immersion experiences to their portfolio, their green-and-outdoorsy brand identity began to feel like a limitation rather than an asset. Prospective students interested in studying Renaissance art in Florence or learning German in Berlin couldn't see themselves in a brand that screamed 'backpacking trip.'

The rebrand began with strategic positioning. Rather than abandoning their adventurous roots entirely, the goal was to elevate the concept of exploration—from physical journeys to intellectual and cultural discovery. The new logo retained a sense of movement and energy but shed the literal hiking references. Clean, modern typography conveyed academic credibility, while dynamic shapes suggested possibility and growth. The bilingual lockup (TUTU FUTURE 徒途学旅) honored their Chinese student audience while signaling their international scope.

Color became a critical tool for differentiation. The old single-green palette was replaced with a flexible system: vibrant blues for language programs, warm terracottas for art and culture, energetic purples for STEM, and yes, a refined green for outdoor experiences. Each program type could have its own visual personality while remaining unmistakably TUTU FUTURE. The mascot—a friendly, curious character—added warmth and approachability, giving the brand a face that could appear across social media, brochures, and promotional materials without feeling corporate or distant.

The impact was immediate. The new brand system gave TUTU FUTURE the visual language to market their full range of programs with confidence. Social media campaigns could now speak to art students, language learners, and STEM enthusiasts with equal authenticity. Printed brochures and digital materials maintained a cohesive look while celebrating the diversity of experiences on offer. The brand had grown up without losing its spirit, ready to guide the next generation of Chinese students on journeys that would shape their futures.

title: Stair Aid
subtitle: an assistive mobility device that enables faster, safer stair navigation for people with temporary lower-limb injuries.
problem: People recovering from lower-limb injuries face a critical mobility challenge: standard crutches force them to navigate stairs slowly and awkwardly, creating safety risks and limiting independence. Traditional crutches require users to adjust length manually—a process that takes 30+ seconds per adjustment and demands both hands. For someone with an injured foot trying to climb stairs, this means choosing between using crutches at the wrong length (unsafe) or stopping to adjust them mid-staircase (impractical). The result is slow, unstable stair navigation that turns a simple task into a frustrating ordeal.
solution: StairAid is a reimagined crutch system designed specifically for stair navigation. The core innovation is a one-handed, trigger-activated length adjustment mechanism that allows users to extend or shorten each crutch in just 3 seconds—8 seconds for a pair. By positioning crutches at uneven lengths (front-back stance), users gain the stability needed to ascend and descend stairs quickly and safely. The curved tip provides a secure stepping point during adjustment and improves balance through increased contact area. A forearm brace replaces the traditional armpit support, reducing fatigue and improving agility on stairs.
body: The challenge began with a simple observation: people on crutches navigate stairs in a fundamentally different way than they walk on flat ground. On level surfaces, crutches are positioned symmetrically at the same length. But on stairs, the optimal stance is diagonal—one crutch higher, one lower—to create a stable tripod with the uninjured leg. Traditional crutches can't adapt to this need without a time-consuming manual adjustment, forcing users to compromise safety for convenience.

The design process started with experimentation. Using standard crutches, real-world stair tests revealed that uneven crutch lengths reduced stair descent time from 8 seconds to 6 seconds and improved stability dramatically. The insight was clear: if users could adjust crutch length instantly, they could optimize for both stair navigation and ground walking without friction. This became the core design objective—develop a length adjustment mechanism that works in seconds, not minutes.

The technical solution evolved through multiple iterations. Early prototypes used an external locking system mounted around the crutch tube, but user feedback revealed aesthetic concerns and mechanical complexity. The second iteration moved the mechanism inside the tube, making it invisible from the outside while reducing part count and improving durability. The locking system uses a lever for linear motion input, a bike cable for motion transfer, and a wedge mechanism to convert vertical hand motion into horizontal locking force. An extension spring keeps the length locked by default, requiring only a trigger pull to release.

Beyond the adjustment mechanism, every detail was optimized for stair use. The curved tip serves dual purposes: it provides a concave surface for applying force during length adjustment and creates a stable stepping point when users need to tilt the crutch on stairs. The forearm brace improves agility compared to traditional armpit supports, allowing users to shift weight dynamically. Material choices—Nylon-66 30-GF for structural components—ensure the design could withstand real-world loads while remaining lightweight. The result is a mobility aid that doesn't just accommodate stair navigation—it's designed for it.

images.caption: Research indicated that the primary cause of chronic ankle instability was the failure of standard crutches to handle stairs safely, leading to the objective of designing a fast, safe, and comfortable stair-navigating mobility aid.

The core innovation relies on uneven crutch lengths, enabling users to adopt a stable front-back stance on stairs. This specific gait ensures 3/4 of the body weight is supported, preventing recurrent injury.
The Stairaid design allows users to seamlessly transition between level ground and stair modes by adjusting and locking the crutch length in just 3 seconds per piece using a quick-release trigger.
The internal locking mechanism utilizes a lever, bike cable, and wedge system to translate vertical hand motion into a horizontal locking pin action, providing secure and rapid length adjustment.

But on stairs, the optimal stance is diagonal—one crutch higher, one lower—to create a stable tripod with the uninjured leg. Traditional crutches can't adapt to this need without a time-consuming manual adjustment, forcing users to compromise safety for convenience.

content.caption: Research indicated that the primary cause of chronic ankle instability was the failure of standard crutches to handle stairs safely, leading to the objective of designing a fast, safe, and comfortable stair-navigating mobility aid.

content.value: The design process started with experimentation. Using standard crutches, real-world stair tests revealed that uneven crutch lengths reduced stair descent time from 8 seconds to 6 seconds and improved stability dramatically. The insight was clear: if users could adjust crutch length instantly, they could optimize for both stair navigation and ground walking without friction. This became the core design objective—develop a length adjustment mechanism that works in seconds, not minutes.

content.caption: The core innovation relies on uneven crutch lengths, enabling users to adopt a stable front-back stance on stairs. This specific gait ensures 3/4 of the body weight is supported, preventing recurrent injury.

content.value: The technical solution evolved through multiple iterations. Early prototypes used an external locking system mounted around the crutch tube, but user feedback revealed aesthetic concerns and mechanical complexity. The second iteration moved the mechanism inside the tube, making it invisible from the outside while reducing part count and improving durability. The locking system uses a lever for linear motion input, a bike cable for motion transfer, and a wedge mechanism to convert vertical hand motion into horizontal locking force. An extension spring keeps the length locked by default, requiring only a trigger pull to release.

content.caption: The Stairaid design allows users to seamlessly transition between level ground and stair modes by adjusting and locking the crutch length in just 3 seconds per piece using a quick-release trigger.

content.value: Beyond the adjustment mechanism, every detail was optimized for stair use. The curved tip serves dual purposes: it provides a concave surface for applying force during length adjustment and creates a stable stepping point when users need to tilt the crutch on stairs. The forearm brace improves agility compared to traditional armpit supports, allowing users to shift weight dynamically. Material choices—Nylon-66 30-GF for structural components—ensure the design could withstand real-world loads while remaining lightweight. The result is a mobility aid that doesn't just accommodate stair navigation—it's designed for it.
